summary: High-level POC scoping for private networking and data residency. Customer requires VPC peering/Privatelink style connectivity, strict EU data residency for EU patients, target latency/throughput goals, and timeline for a two-week POC with bench runs. Redwood AE+SE explained options and next steps to run benchmarks and share security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Mark (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Mark from Redwood Inference, AE on this account. We also have Priya from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Sarah (NovusCare/CTO): Doing good, thanks. We've got Tom and Nina on from infra and security. Short on time but excited to scope this POC.
[00:16] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, we'll run through connectivity options, success criteria, and a benchmark plan. Quick note — apologies in advance for any transcript artefacts, auto captions sometimes say privatelink as private linked, ha.
[00:26] Tom (NovusCare - Infra): No worries. For context, our production lives in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. We need EU patient data to never egress EU boundaries.
[00:36] Mark: Got it. Primary asks we heard were private networking (VPC peering or PrivateLink), region control, and clear egress rules. Is that accurate?
[00:43] Sarah: Yes. Also latency target — we want p99 inference under 200ms for text-generation flows, and throughput to support bursts to ~100 requests per second during peak for the POC.
[00:52] Priya: OK that's helpful. For POC we usually run a benchmark harness: synthetic traffic, peak and steady-state, tail latency and token cost estimates. Would you be able to provide a representative traffic profile?
[01:02] Eli (NovusCare - ML): We can export 24h of request traces and a 1GB seed dataset with prompts.
[01:08] Mark: Perfect. For network options: we support VPC Peering (for customers hosting in same cloud and account topology), AWS PrivateLink (or GCP equivalent) for private endpoint-style, and also customer-hosted transit with route tables. Each has tradeoffs — peering is simpler for full L3 reachability, PrivateLink is better for restricted egress and allowlisting.
[01:25] Tom: If we do PrivateLink, do we have to accept egress through a non-EU host? Concern is that the PrivateLink endpoint must be in the same region; we need EU endpoints for EU traffic only.
[01:33] Priya: Yes, we can provision private endpoints in eu-west-1 and restrict routing so EU traffic stays in region. For hosted POC infra we can spin up dedicated capacity in eu-west-1. No EU traffic will leave region if we configure the peering and route tables correctly and we sign the data residency agreement.
[01:44] Nina (Security): We also need KMS integration and customer-managed keys. Are you able to integrate with AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault?
[01:51] Mark: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations; we'll share the details in the security runbook.
[01:55] Speaker 1: um ok yeah
[02:00] Priya: For benchmarking, suggested plan: week 1 — network setup and connectivity test (VPC peering or PrivateLink), week 1 end — dry-run benchmarks with small dataset, week 2 — full load tests with 10k requests, latency p95/p99 measurement, and model quality checks. POC length typically two weeks.
[02:18] Sarah: Two weeks works. Success criteria from our side: p99 <200ms, throughput ~100 rps with acceptable cost per 1k tokens, model accuracy stable against our eval set, and no data egress outside assigned regions.
[02:28] Mark: We'll codify that as the success checklist. Also we'll include model fallbacks and routing policies in case of capacity constraints.
[02:35] Tom: On the infra side we need a stable egress IP or range that we can allowlist in our firewall for outgoing connections to Redwood endpoints. How does that look with PrivateLink?
[02:43] Priya: With PrivateLink, egress is via the interface endpoint inside your VPC so outbound from your infra to the endpoint is private. For the egress to our service plane, if you're on Dedicated we can allocate fixed egress IPs or we can provide NAT traverse details. For hosted PrivateLink endpoints the traffic stays in region and we can provide the endpoint ID; but fixed public egress IP is a Dedicated feature.
[03:02] Nina: OK, so for strict allowlist we might need dedicated capacity. We'll flag that.
[03:07] Sarah: What about audit logs and retention for the POC? We have to keep request logs for 90 days for a compliance check.
[03:14] Mark: We can enable audit logs and export them to your S3, and retention is configurable. We'll include the steps.
[03:20] Tom: Are there any changes required to our VPC peering route tables that could cause asymmetric routing? We want to avoid hairpinning across AZs.
[03:27] Priya: We'll provide a network diagram and recommended route table entries, including the IP ranges to avoid. There can be nuances with cross-account peering but we've documented common pitfalls.
[03:37] Eli: Regarding workload sizing — what GPU config are you recommending for our expected throughput?
[03:42] Priya: For the models you described (ca. 7B footprint fine-tuned), a single A100-style GPU (or M60 equivalent depending on quant) can sustain roughly 80–150 rps depending on sequence length and batching. For consistent p99 <200ms at 100 rps we usually recommend starting with a 2-GPU Dedicated pool for the POC to give headroom, or a high-concurrency hosted instance if you want faster setup but slightly higher variable cost.
[04:05] Tom: Do you support quantized variants to reduce memory and increase throughput?
[04:09] Priya: Yes, we support int8 and dynamic quantization paths. We'll recommend a quant profile based on your eval prompts. That typically lowers GPU RAM needs and increases throughput by 20–40% but can slightly affect generations — we include quality checks in the benchmark.
[04:23] Sarah: Benchmarks — what exactly do you need from us for the test?
[04:26] Mark: We'll need a 1GB seed dataset for the prompts, a traffic profile (requests per minute distribution), any eval prompts and their expected outputs for accuracy checks, and an allowlist of CIDR blocks or confirmation you'd like Dedicated with fixed egress IP.
[04:39] Nina: We'll send the seed dataset and the compliance doc list. One question — encryption in transit and at rest both required?
[04:46] Mark: Yes. TLS for transit and KMS for rest. We'll map how to attach your KMS keys to the storage bucket and model snapshots.
[04:52] Speaker 2: [crosstalk] yep
[04:55] Priya: On timelines: if we get artifacts by Friday (2026-10-23), we can stand up network connectivity and an initial benchmark the following week (week of 2026-10-26). Full POC wrap in two weeks. Does that timeline align with your internal approvals?
[05:07] Sarah: We can aim to sign the POC SOW by Thursday. Procurement is fast for pilot-sized contracts.
[05:12] Tom: For the bench test, can Redwood run an agent inside our VPC to generate traffic, or do you prefer we run the client-side harness?
[05:19] Priya: Either works. We often provide a lightweight client harness you can run inside your VPC to generate traffic and hit the private endpoint. If you prefer Redwood to run from our side we'll simulate from the same region but that wouldn't exercise private peering paths — so recommend running the harness inside your VPC for the network test.
[05:33] Eli: We'll run the harness. Can you share the repo and config?
[05:36] Priya: Yes, we'll share a GitHub link with scripts and a sample terraform for endpoint provisioning.
[05:41] Mark: Alright let's capture the success criteria again: p99 <200ms, throughput 100 rps sustained at peak, model outputs match our eval set within agreed thresholds, no EU egress for EU traffic, KMS integration for at-rest encryption, audit logs exported to our S3, and final cost estimate within the budget you shared.
[05:57] Nina: That sounds right. Also we need to confirm retention and deletion policy for the POC data after completion.
[06:03] Mark: We'll include a data deletion plan in the SOW and provide a certificate of deletion upon request.
[06:07] Speaker 1: um okay
[06:10] Sarah: Any blockers from Redwood's side we should be aware of?
[06:13] Priya: No major blockers; dedicated capacity is request-based but we can provision for a small pilot quickly. The only time sink is procurement and legal signoff on the data residency addendum.
[06:24] Tom: Security question — SSO and RBAC integration; can we map our Okta groups to Redwood roles?
[06:31] Mark: Yes, SAML/Okta supported. We'll provide a role mapping guide.
[06:36] Eli: For the benchmark we'll need a synthetic user session distribution: bursty traffic with median 60 rps and peaks 120 rps.
[06:43] Priya: Noted. We'll parameterize the harness for that distribution and run multiple iterations to capture p95/p99.
[06:49] Sarah: Anything else on the data residency piece? We're strict — if a request originates from EU we want guaranteed EU processing and storage.
[06:58] Priya: We can route EU-origin requests to eu-west-1 only and pin model variants there. For model artifacts we will host snapshots in EU storage buckets and ensure KMS key is EU-located. We'll include region-pinning config in the runbook.
[07:10] Tom: Network nit — do you support inter-AZ endpoint redundancy?
[07:13] Priya: Yes, endpoints can be provisioned per AZ or multi-AZ depending on your tolerance. Multi-AZ reduces single-AZ blast radius.
[07:21] Sarah: Ok good. On success measurement: who signs off? Will NovusCare CISO or the CTO sign?
[07:27] Nina: Security will do the compliance checks, and CTO will approve overall. We'll confirm signoff matrix in the SOW.
[07:34] Mark: We'll include an acceptance criteria table in the SOW.
[07:38] Speaker 2: [small laugh] cool
[07:41] Priya: Any objections or red flags from the customer side?
[07:44] Sarah: Not at this point. Two things — cost expectations and fixed egress IPs — we flagged.
[07:50] Mark: We'll include dedicated capacity pricing and an option for reserved egress IPs in the pricing sheet.
[07:55] Eli: For the POC we'll accept estimated pricing — final enterprise terms later.
[07:59] Mark: Sounds good. I'll capture action items.
[08:03] Mark: Recap of action items: share security docs, share harness repo, customer to send dataset/traffic profile, schedule bench window.
[08:10] Sarah: Great. Let's aim to reconvene after the network setup in 48–72 hours.
[08:16] Priya: We'll send the runbook and links by tomorrow.
[08:19] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[08:21] Nina: Thank you.
[08:23] Mark: Thanks all, talk soon.
[08:25] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: minor auto-caption errors, occasional speaker label as Speaker 1/2, some run-on sentences preserved.

Benchmark plan (inline):
- Connectivity test: basic curl/handshake to private endpoint, check TLS and KMS handshake (Day 1).
- Dry-run: 10k short requests spread over 30 minutes to validate p50/p95.
- Full load: multi-hour run with burst patterns (median 60 rps, peak 120 rps) capturing p99 and token costs.
- Quality checks: run 200 evaluation prompts against golden outputs and compute acceptance metrics.

Network provisioning notes (inline):
- PrivateLink: interface endpoints in eu-west-1 and us-east-1, route tables updated to point to endpoints, security groups to restrict ports.
- VPC Peering: cross-account peering with explicit route entries, avoid overlapping CIDRs, NAT recommendations for egress IP control.
- Dedicated capacity option: provides fixed egress IPs for allowlist; requires additional provisioning lead time.

POC timeline (proposed):
- 2026-10-22: Redwood sends runbook + security docs + pricing.
- 2026-10-23: NovusCare provides dataset, traffic profile, and required compliance doc list.
- 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-30: Network setup + dry-run + full benchmarks.
- 2026-10-30: POC wrap and acceptance review (two-week pilot window from initial setup).
notes: Realistic sales scoping call with AE+SE; strong emphasis on EU data residency, PrivateLink vs peering tradeoffs, egress IP allowlisting, KMS and audit logs. Action items and next steps captured.
